newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hashimoto and Communists win in Tokyo elections.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto and Communists win in Tokyo elections.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and the Japanese Communist Party (JCP) both made significant gains on Sunday in Tokyo local government elections.
The biggest loser was the country's main national opposition party Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) which did not win a single seat.

The contest for 127 seats in the Tokyo Metropolitan Assembly of 23 inner-city boroughs, suburban municipalities, rural districts and outlying Pacific islands was regarded as a test of voter mood in the country's largest city.
Voters for the Tokyo assembly poll numbered 9.4 million, some 10 percent of nationwide electors.
The next national-level elections are due to be held in July 1998 for half of the 252 seats in parliament's Upper House, a less influential chamber than the Lower House.
Results announced by the Election Administration Commission showed the LDP won 54 seats to maintain its status as the top party in the assembly, up from 38 seats before the election.
The JCP came second with 26 seats, twice its pre-election strength, in the latest strong showing by communists in local government elections.
It was the communists' best performance ever in a Tokyo Metropolitan Assembly election, beating its previous record of 24 seats in the 1973 poll.
However the communists have been unable so far to translate their success in local government elections, which are fought mainly on parochial issues,into success in national polls.
The Buddhist-backed Komeito (Clean Government Party) lost its status as the number two party in the assembly although all of its 24 candidates won their seats.
The New Frontier Party, which held four seats in the old assembly and contested 11 seats, came away empty-handed in the latest sign of its declining strength as a political force.
The setback was likely to increase pressure on party chief Ichiro Ozawa to resign to stem a series of election defeats and defections to other parties.
The remaining seats were won by a mixture of small parties and independent candidates, reflecting the turmoil that has swept Japanese politics for the past few years.
Voter turnout was a record low 40.80 percent, below the previous record of 51.43 percent in the last 1993 poll.
A record heat wave which gripped most of Japan on the weekend was blamed for the low turnout.
Kazuo Shii, chief of the JCP Secretariat, said his party's gains reflected voter criticism of "all ruling-party politics."
